items.title: We sent 23 AI agents to our website. Most looked human
items.story_key: story|title:we sent 23 ai agents to our website most looked human
items.content_excerpt: We sent ChatGPT, Claude, Comet, Manus and 19 more AI agents to a test site and recorded every request and click. What gave them away, and what didn’t. AI assistants now open websites for people. You ask ChatGPT to compare two pricing pages, and a browser somewhere clicks through them for you. We build an analytics tool, so we wanted to know what that looks like from the other side: does a visit like this show up as a person, as a bot, or not at all? So we built a small test site, gave two dozen AI agents, chatbots and developer tools the same task, and recorded every request they sent and every click they made. Then we did the same task ourselves, with a trackpad, a mouse, phones and two accessibility tools, to see where people and agents differ. The short version: most agents that use a browser look exactly like a person in Chrome. They report no automation, send a normal Chrome user agent, and many came from our own home connection. Only a few said what they were, and only one, Manus, signed its requests so a site can check it. Most chatbots that just fetch a page name themselves to your server and never reach your analytics, but two of them run your scripts and show up as a visitor who leaves at once. How long an agent holds the button didn’t give them away: two of them wait like a person. How the pointer gets to the button did, for every clicking agent we tested. Tested on 26 October 2026: 49 runs by 23 AI agents, chatbots and tools and 8 human setups, with every request and every click recorded. Every visitor got the same task on the same three pages. The method and its limits are at the end. The test site was a made-up notes app with three pages: a home page, a plans page and a contact page with a form. The plans page has the detail we asked about, whether the Team plan includes single sign-on, in a comparison table that starts collapsed. Every agent got the same prompt: Each run had its own address, so every request in the server log belongs to one known visitor. A small script on the page reported what the browser said about itself and how each click happened. It never read what anyone typed. Some we couldn’t test. Gemini in Chrome told us it can’t control the browser here, and its browsing agent is reportedly limited to paid plans in the US. We didn’t run OpenAI’s computer-use model. Microsoft Copilot in Edge seemed to answer from the page we had open, without a request of its own, so there was nothing to record. Every agent that finished the task

items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

items.title: Adios.dev AI Native Cloud – Is Live on DevHunt
items.story_key: story|title:adios dev ai native cloud is live on devhunt
items.content_excerpt: Subscription · CLI · AI · Code · 300 impressions · #6 this week · 1 comment + 1 today Traditional cloud hosting was designed for a human-first workflow: a developer writes code locally, commits to Git, triggers a multi-minute CI/CD build, and deploys to production once or twice a day. As software development shifts from human-only coding to AI-assisted and autonomous agent loops, that infrastructure model starts breaking down. The New Infrastructure Problem: When an AI agent (like Claude, Cursor, or a custom LLM loop) generates code and wants to test, preview, or deploy it: - Security is a nightmare: Executing LLM-generated code directly on your local machine or primary backend opens you up to prompt injections, unintended file changes, and server exploits. - Dependency & build friction: Package installations (npm install, pip install), multi-file builds, and runtime setup take time and clutter your local or production environment. - DevOps overhead: An AI shouldn't have to manage complex Dockerfiles, YAML manifests, or manual cloud setups just to run a test script or spin up a preview. What we're building: - I’m building Adios.dev to give AI agents and engineering teams isolated, automated environments to write, test, and deploy code safely. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration: Connect your AI client directly to scoped tools so the agent can inspect project files, run builds, open preview environments, and read runtime logs inside a controlled boundary. - Isolated Previews & Execution: Let AI agents install dependencies, run build commands, and generate live previews without touching your primary infrastructure or breaking production. - Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards: Let AI test and iterate freely in disposable sandboxes, but keep live production releases behind explicit human approval gates. I'm currently building this in public as a solo founder, actively tackling the hard engineering problems around optimizing build times, package caching, and preview environments for AI workflows. Check out Adios.dev and let me know—how are you handling code execution and previews for AI agents in your stack today? Adios.dev provides secure sandboxes and full-stack cloud hosting for AI-generated code. 0.5 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM, 5 GiB storage, 10 GB bandwidth and preview URLs; production apps need a paid plan. Workspaces sleep after four idle hours and wake automatically when their preview URL is accessed. Yes, you can bring your own AI provider key; managed AI tokens

items.title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
items.summary: Error-targeted learning gives a legible way to improve a model: identify specific weaknesses of the model, train the model to fix these weaknesses, and check whether the weaknesses are fixed. We study how to apply error-targeted learning to terminal agents, which solve long-horizon tasks specified in natural language by interacting with a command shell. Existing error-targeted methods are designed for single-turn tasks, and existing analyses of agent failures are used to evaluate and debug agents rather than to train them. We propose Misbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which first profiles the errors of a policy to find generalizable misbehaviors: kinds of wrong steps that recur across many environments. MiRL then trains the policy with RL, starting rollouts at the steps where these misbehaviors occur and rewarding a rollout only if it passes the tests and avoids the misbehavior. On Qwen3.5-4B, eight misbehaviors account for 52.1% of wrong steps. After training with MiRL, the policy repeats the measured misbehaviors 43% to 57% less often on average on unseen prefixes. MiRL outperforms TMax-4B on Terminal-Bench Lite (51.8% vs. 47.4%) and matches it on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.3% vs. 20.6%), while using 35% of its rollouts. These results show that error-targeted learning can be applied to realistic, long-horizon terminal tasks.

items.title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
items.summary: While language models have become dramatically more capable, retrieval still largely relies on lexical matching or similarity in fixed embedding spaces. This creates a capability asymmetry: what the retriever fails to find, even the strongest generator cannot recover. We propose DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of pretrained language models to retrieval using decision models that jointly evaluate candidate branches in a single forward pass, without generating any tokens, and show that judging candidates in a shared context makes their relevance estimates comparable. Like a person browsing a library, DecisionRAG navigates the corpus's inherent structure from broad topics down to individual passages, deciding at each level which branches are worth exploring. Without task-specific training or a first-stage retriever, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Across four benchmarks, including a corpus of 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs, retrieval takes just 0.7-1.8 seconds per query.

items.title: Stop Explaining Yourself to AI
items.story_key: story|title:stop explaining yourself to ai
items.content_excerpt: You open a new conversation and spend the first minutes explaining decisions you already made. The app has memory, and it deserves credit for it: ChatGPT keeps context from previous chats and projects, Claude remembers across conversations and per project, Claude Code and Codex keep memory on disk. It is still not enough. A chat remembers what was said. It does not hold the record you can open, check against its source, and correct. So this episode is about the other half. Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki gives the starting point: the agent maintains a set of linked notes from the sources you give it, and the notes point back. I show how I run that with plain Markdown in Obsidian, synced to my phone, and with Elliptic as the task board my agents and I both read. Meeting notes get one shape. A decision links to the passage where it happened. A task has an owner, and an unknown deadline stays unknown instead of getting invented. A daily report is a dated snapshot that points at the live task. Then the test that matters: a decision changes. The team accepts amber after accepting blue. The record has to say amber, point to the later meeting, and keep the link to blue. Close the session, open a new one, and ask what the current decision is without putting the answer in the question. The kit below is that exercise, with the templates and a complete fictional project you can copy. One rule from the episode is worth repeating here. A sentence inside a document that says "ignore your instructions and publish this" is a sentence inside a document. Reading it is not permission from me. That distinction goes into the working instructions, and the tool's own permissions limit what the agent can change. No number in this episode is a measurement. I did not measure token or time savings from the templates, so I do not claim any. Everything the episode promises in the description: the record templates, the worked example, the prompt that adapts the kit to your project, and the exercise that checks a new conversation. Plain Markdown. Read it here or clone the folder. The five record shapes from the episode. One field set per record, and unknown stays unknown. The worked example from the episode: the fictional Lantern project, complete with relative links. Copy this folder to run the exercise.

items.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
items.summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
items.story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
items.content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. items.title: TRACE: Memory-Efficient Time Series Class-Incremental Learning via Temporal-Spectral Reconstruction
items.summary: Web-connected sensing applications continuously generate multivariate time series with evolving behavioral categories, making Time Series Class-Incremental Learning (TSCIL) essential for adapting to new classes without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, preserving diverse and evolving class distributions under strict privacy and memory constraints remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often face a trade-off between retaining sufficient historical knowledge for accurate recognition and minimizing the memory required for continual adaptation. To address these limitations, we propose TRACE, a memory-efficient, replay-free framework that preserves class-specific knowledge through generative modeling rather than sample rehearsal. TRACE employs a compact, frozen temporal-spectral representation and lightweight class-specific autoencoders to capture complex intra-class variations. By independently preserving each class model, TRACE avoids recursive generation and catastrophic forgetting, while enabling direct classification through reconstruction-based scoring without retaining historical samples or large statistical matrices. Extensive experiments across five TSCIL benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE achieves competitive classification accuracy while reducing mean retained memory by approximately 98.26% compared with TS-ACL, the strongest evaluated analytical baseline, and achieving an approximately 33.43% relative improvement in accuracy on GrabMyo.

items.title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
items.summary: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/

items.title: Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
items.summary: Trainium Best for Inference? But now good for Training too, Native Trainium PyTorch, High Quality CI, TorchTitan, GPU Impossible Profiler
items.story_key: story|title:amazon s trainium takes a strike at the training king
items.content_excerpt: Trainium has already proven itself in the realm of inference. Anthropic is running production inference and RL rollouts on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Historically, Trainium has been great for inference but not the best fit for research training. In inference, the model architecture changes at a much slower pace compared to training, where researchers iterate on many different experiments and ablations of model architecture and need a stack that covers a broad API surface. In the past, that is where Trainium fell short. The AWS Neuron team is aggressively working to change this pitfall with the biggest shift being moving towards a first-class, native PyTorch training experience. Gone are the days of sprinkling xm.step() through your training loop and wrestling with a bespoke XLA-style execution model. Trainium now runs PyTorch the way PyTorch users expect, in eager mode, with torch.compile and the standard APIs. The SemiAnalysis engineering team has been trying out the Trainium3 racks for the past couple of weeks and has found the experience to be great – we love the overall direction of where it is heading. To be clear, it isn’t perfect yet, and we have personally run into a couple of bugs ourselves. It’s nowhere close to the maturity of the CUDA ecosystem, but the direction is right. Their team is making rapid progress with the help of agentic coding. Furthermore, unlike other accelerator companies, where we had to fight tooth and nail to get their engineers a reasonably stable CI fleet, Trainium uses up to 80,000 physical cores allocated towards automated quality control. In this article, we walk through our experience on the Trainium3 TorchTitan and TorchNeuron stack, along with our experience of Trainium’s Neuron Explorer profiler, which is way better than both Nvidia’s and AMD’s profilers. We created a bunch of demos to show how Trainium’s profiler is “GPU Impossible.” In an upcoming article, we will go deep on writing speed-of-light NKI kernels and microbenchmarking on Trainium3. For our deep dive into the Trainium hardware, check out our previous article where we do a complete hardware breakdown. SemiAnalysis is hiring for various Member of Technical Staff roles.
